extracted.intended_audience: pipeline operators, industry compliance officers, and pipeline safety regulators
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory requirements and evaluation criteria for installing, testing, maintaining, and investigating remote/alternative valve technologies (RMVs, ASVs, RCVs, manual alternatives) and for emergency/rupture notification and response on gas and hazardous liquid pipelines. Covers drill requirements, post-failure actions, failure investigation elements, 9-1-1 notification, HCA evaluations, installation applicability, and related documentation/notification procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual valve annual drill applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual drills apply to manually operated valves used as alternative equivalent technology only, and not to ASVs or RCVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA intended annual drills to include manual operation of a local actuator or closing via a hand-wheel. Annual drills are not required for every manual valve; rather, one randomly selected manual valve in each of the operator's field work units must be drilled annually. The operator may determine the random selection method, but that selection method must be included in written procedures so it can be inspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual valve drill operation minimum closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Full closure of a manually operated valve is not required for the valve maintenance demonstration; at minimum, a 25 percent closure of the valve is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA determined that overcoming inertia is often the most difficult part of operating a valve; 25% (or more) closure is sufficient to demonstrate operability/functionality while allowing operators to maintain service without major interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on tabletop drills for manual valve response times
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabletop (paper) drills are not allowed to verify response times for manually operated valves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA believes tabletop exercises cannot effectively confirm real-time travel time to a valve location or the time needed to manually close a valve under rupture conditions. Operators must physically arrive at and operate the manual valve to verify functionality and meet closure-time requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-failed-drill timelines and remedial actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a failed drill, operators must identify alternative shut-off measures within 7 days and repair the valve within 12 months (final rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA originally thought 7 days to identify alternatives and 6 months to repair were appropriate, but extended the repair period to 12 months in the final rule. Operators may request, in advance of undertaking repairs, an extension of the 12-month repair period by demonstrating that repair within the rule's timeline is economically, technically, or operationally infeasible (e.g., prohibitive costs, difficulty securing access/permits, long procurement lead times, component/labor availability). PHMSA declined to offer a similar notification/extension process for the 7-day identification requirement, emphasizing prompt identification is essential to protect the public/environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative equivalent technology shut-off coverage and closure time
rubrics_metrics.description: Any alternative compliant RMV or equivalent technology must contain the entire shut-off segment and comply with the rule's valve closure time standard (30-minute standard referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA did not intend to require that valves identified as alternative compliant RMVs based on a failed drill comply with valve spacing requirements; however, any alternative compliant RMV must still meet the closure-time standard and contain the entire shut-off segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure investigation procedures and sample testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must establish procedures for analyzing accidents and failures, including selection of samples of failed facilities or equipment for laboratory examination where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post-incident analysis should identify potential operations and maintenance (O&M) measures to reduce or limit release volume and damage from similar future events. Reviews should address factors including detection and mitigation actions, response time, valve location, valve actuation, and SCADA system performance. PHMSA retained (and clarified) the authority to require selection of samples for laboratory testing when appropriate to identify safety issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-incident analysis content and incorporation of lessons learned
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon completing a post-incident or failure analysis, operators must develop and implement lessons learned across their procedures and programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lessons learned should be incorporated into operator personnel training and qualification programs and into design, construction, testing, maintenance, operations, and emergency procedure manuals and specifications. PHMSA modified wording from “P&M measures” to “operations and maintenance measures” to avoid confusion with other integrity management terms, and notes operators are not expected to implement measures that are clearly unreasonable or impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation, senior executive certification, and recordkeeping for failure investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure investigations require documentation, senior executive review/certification, and recordkeeping to ensure quality and implementation of findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry commenters argued for limiting application to final analyses to avoid undue burdens; PHMSA emphasized that senior executive certification is essential to ensure investigation quality and to highlight the importance of implementing results. The final analysis (conclusion) is the appropriate subject of certification and long-term retention to avoid excessive preliminary recordkeeping burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rupture identification and documentation of method
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must define and document their method for 'rupture identification' (the point when the operator has sufficient information reasonably to determine a rupture), triggered by a 'notification of potential rupture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule defines 'notification of potential rupture' and requires operators to document in their operations manual or written procedures the method for rupture identification. After identifying a rupture, operators must close RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies necessary to isolate the ruptured pipeline segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency procedures: rupture mitigation and liaison with 9-1-1/public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators' emergency procedures must provide for rupture mitigation and require contacting and maintaining liaison with the appropriate public safety answering point (9-1-1) when a potential rupture is notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA clarified the requirement applies to all notifications of potential ruptures on gas and hazardous liquid systems covered by emergency planning regs. Where 9-1-1 service is unavailable, operators must establish adequate means of communication with fire, police, and other public officials. Operators may liaise with an emergency response coordinating agency (e.g., 9-1-1 centers or county emergency managers) instead of contacting each individual jurisdictional responder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator responsibilities to identify jurisdictions and contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must learn the responsibilities, resources, jurisdictional areas, and emergency contact numbers for each Federal, State, and local government organization that may respond to a pipeline emergency, and inform such officials of the operator's ability to respond and communicate during pipeline emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To meet the rule, operators must determine which government organizations may respond to pipeline emergencies involving their facilities and maintain liaison/communications pathways; this applies regardless of 9-1-1 availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASV/RCV/EFRD evaluation requirements for HCAs
rubrics_metrics.description: When ASVs, RCVs, or EFRDs are installed as protective measures for High Consequence Areas (HCAs) such that they function as RMVs, operators must be able to evaluate and demonstrate they can identify a rupture within 10 minutes and meet the RMV closure time and associated maintenance requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA proposed no new requirements other than that valves functionally treated as RMVs via risk analysis must meet the 10-minute rupture identification standard, the valve closure time standard, and maintenance requirements. Operators performing such risk analyses should consider rupture detection (not just leak detection) speed and ensure cybersecurity and other operational concerns are considered (PHMSA notes cyber risk but recognizes regulatory authority limits; coordination with TSA/CISA exists at federal level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification requirements for use of alternative equivalent technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators seeking to use alternative equivalent technology must submit advance notification to PHMSA with a site-specific technical and safety evaluation demonstrating equivalent level of safety to an RMV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluation must reference factors including: design, construction, maintenance and operating procedures; technology design and operational characteristics (e.g., operation/closure times for manual valves); service reliability and life; accessibility to operator personnel; nearby population density; and potential consequences to the environment and public. For manual valves used as alternatives, the notification must also demonstrate site-specific economic, technical, or operational infeasibility of installing an RMV (e.g., lack of communications/power, terrain, prohibitive cost, labor/component availability, inability to secure access/permits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project-specific requests for compliance deadline extension
rubrics_metrics.description: An operator may submit a project-specific advance notification requesting extension of a compliance deadline, demonstrating that installing an RMV or alternative equivalent technology in connection with near-term construction/replacement projects would be economically, technically, or operationally infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations can reference prohibitive economic costs, difficulty securing access rights, component/labor availability and procurement lead times, or permitting requirements. PHMSA retains discretion under §192.18 to accept or reject such requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: RMV/alternative technology installation applicability and valve spacing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies are required on onshore gas pipeline segments (diameter >= 6 inches) that are newly constructed or meet the 'entirely replaced' definition after April 10, 2023; RMVs/alternatives installed under §192.179 must meet operational requirements and (in some statements) valve spacing requirements of that section, with certain exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Installation requirements do not apply to pipeline segments in Class 1 or Class 2 locations with a PIR <= 150 feet. For entirely replaced onshore segments, requirements apply only when replacement projects involve addition, replacement, or removal of a valve. Operators replacing pipeline segments are not required to meet spacing if the distance from any point to the nearest valve does not exceed specified distances (4 miles in Class 4, 7.5 miles in Class 3, 10 miles in other locations). PHMSA also clarified elsewhere that valves identified as alternative RMVs based on a failed drill are not required to meet valve spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve installation on class location change and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: When class location changes require complying with maximum allowable operating pressure requirements, operators must install valves (including RMVs/alternative equivalents) as necessary; such valves must be installed within 24 months of the class location change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an operator replaces less than 2 miles of pipe in a 5-mile contiguous stretch during 24 months to meet pressure requirements, the operator must either comply with valve spacing at §192.179(a) or install/use RMVs/alternatives so the entirety of the replaced segment is between 2 RMVs/alternatives and distance between those valves does not exceed 20 miles. Operators are not required to comply if they replace less than 1,000 feet within any single contiguous mile within 24 months.
